title: Production Deployment of Microservices on GCP Cloud Run
description: A hands-on DevOps course covering serverless container deployment on Google Cloud Run, Direct VPC egress, Cloud SQL integration, Secret Manager, revision traffic splitting, and cold-start mitigation.
body: Deploy production containerized workloads on Google Cloud Run. Master multi-stage Docker builds, gcloud deployment CLI commands, Direct VPC egress networking for internal database communication, Secret Manager bindings, safe revision rollouts with traffic splitting, and cold-start mitigation.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: Building Minimal Multi-Stage Docker Images
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A 900MB Image and a 12-Second Cold Start

Your first Cloud Run deployment used `FROM golang:1.22` all the way through. It works, but the image is 900MB. Every scale-from-zero cold start now takes 12 seconds to pull and start the container — long enough that your uptime monitor flags it as a failed health check, and users hitting a cold instance see a visible hang.

A multi-stage build compiles in a full-featured builder image, then copies only the final static binary into a minimal runtime image:

```dockerfile
# --- Build stage ---
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/server ./cmd/server

# --- Final stage ---
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=builder /out/server /server
USER nonroot:nonroot
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
```

```text
  golang:1.22 (900MB) ──build──►  binary  ──copy──►  distroless/static (~15MB total)
         │                                                    │
         └─ discarded after build ─── never shipped ──────────┘
```

Shrinking from 900MB to under 20MB cuts image-pull time dramatically — the single biggest lever for reducing Cloud Run's scale-from-zero cold start latency, addressed further with `--min-instances` in Lesson 2.3.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: On Cloud Run specifically, image size directly affects cold-start time because the platform must pull the image before starting your container — this is a bigger cold-start lever here than in a long-running Kubernetes cluster where images are usually already cached on nodes.

sections.title: Section 2: Production Deployment & Direct VPC Egress

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Production `gcloud run deploy` Specification
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Deploy Command That Silently Skips Health Checks

A teammate deploys with a bare `gcloud run deploy --image ...` and no resource limits. The service works fine in testing, then falls over in production under real traffic because it was allocated the platform default of 512Mi memory and 1 vCPU — nowhere near enough for a service holding a database connection pool.

A production deploy command should be explicit about every dimension that affects cost, latency, and reliability:

```bash
gcloud run deploy gg-cms-backend \
  --image gcr.io/ggcms/backend:1.4.2 \
  --region us-central1 \
  --platform managed \
  --memory 512Mi \
  --cpu 1 \
  --min-instances 1 \
  --max-instances 10 \
  --concurrency 80 \
  --timeout 30 \
  --network default \
  --subnet default \
  --vpc-egress private-ranges-only \
  --set-secrets "DB_WRITE_URL=gg-cms-db-write-url:latest" \
  --set-env-vars "LOG_LEVEL=info" \
  --no-traffic \
  --tag candidate
```

Each flag answers a specific production question:

| Flag | Question it answers |
| :--- | :--- |
| `--min-instances 1` | "Do we accept cold starts, or keep at least one warm instance?" |
| `--concurrency 80` | "How many simultaneous requests can one instance safely handle?" (tune to your service's actual CPU/memory profile — don't leave the 80 default unexamined) |
| `--timeout 30` | "How long before Cloud Run kills a hung request?" |
| `--no-traffic` + `--tag candidate` | "Deploy this revision WITHOUT routing production traffic to it yet" — see Lesson 2.3 |

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: `--no-traffic --tag candidate` is the single most important pair of flags for safe production deploys — it separates "deploy a new revision" from "send it traffic," which is what makes staged rollouts (Lesson 2.3) possible at all.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Connecting Cloud Run to Private Cloud SQL / Compute Engine VMs
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Database IP Exposed to the Public Internet

The fastest way to connect Cloud Run to a database is to give the Cloud SQL instance a public IP and let Cloud Run reach it over the internet. It works — until a security review flags that your production database is now reachable from any IP on earth, protected only by a password.

**Direct VPC egress** routes Cloud Run's outbound traffic through your VPC's private RFC 1918 address space instead, so the database connection never touches the public internet:

```bash
gcloud run deploy gg-cms-backend \
  --image gcr.io/ggcms/backend:1.4.2 \
  --network default \
  --subnet default \
  --vpc-egress private-ranges-only \
  --set-secrets "DB_WRITE_URL=gg-cms-db-write-url:latest"
```

```text
  ┌─────────────────┐   private VPC route   ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Cloud Run        │ ─────────────────────► │ Cloud SQL             │
  │ (--vpc-egress    │   (10.x.x.x, RFC 1918) │ (private IP only,     │
  │  private-ranges- │                        │  no public IP at all) │
  │  only)           │                        └──────────────────────┘
  └─────────────────┘
         │
         │ public internet traffic (e.g. calling a third-party API)
         ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ Internet          │  ← unaffected: private-ranges-only means ONLY RFC 1918
  │                   │    traffic goes through the VPC; public API calls still
  └─────────────────┘    egress normally
```

`--vpc-egress private-ranges-only` is deliberately narrow: it routes only RFC 1918 private-range traffic through the VPC connector, leaving calls to public APIs (Stripe, SendGrid, etc.) unaffected. The alternative, `--vpc-egress all-traffic`, routes everything through the VPC — useful if you need all egress to appear from a static IP via Cloud NAT, but adds VPC connector cost and latency to every outbound call, including ones that didn't need it.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: Removing the Cloud SQL instance's public IP entirely (not just relying on firewall rules) is the real security win here — a firewall rule is one misconfiguration away from being disabled, but an instance with no public IP has no public attack surface to misconfigure.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Revision Traffic Splitting & Cold-Start Mitigation
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Bad Deploy That Hit 100% of Traffic Instantly

By default, `gcloud run deploy` immediately routes 100% of production traffic to the newly deployed revision. If that revision has a bug — a bad migration, a broken environment variable — every single user hits it at once, with no gradual exposure and no easy way to compare it against the previous, known-good revision.

### Staged Rollout with Traffic Splitting

```bash
# 1. Deploy the new revision WITHOUT routing any traffic to it
gcloud run deploy gg-cms-backend \
  --image gcr.io/ggcms/backend:1.5.0 \
  --no-traffic \
  --tag candidate

# 2. Send 5% of production traffic to the candidate, keep 95% on the current revision
gcloud run services update-traffic gg-cms-backend \
  --to-tags candidate=5

# 3. Watch error rates / latency for the candidate tag specifically, then ramp up
gcloud run services update-traffic gg-cms-backend \
  --to-tags candidate=50

# 4. Once confident, send 100% of traffic to the new revision
gcloud run services update-traffic gg-cms-backend \
  --to-latest

# Rollback is instantaneous if step 3 shows problems — just repoint traffic:
gcloud run services update-traffic gg-cms-backend \
  --to-revisions gg-cms-backend-00042-abc=100
```

```text
  Revision N-1 (stable)  ◄── 95% traffic ──┐
                                            │
  Revision N (candidate) ◄── 5% traffic ───┤  gradually shift %
         │                                  │  as confidence grows
         └── bad error rate? ───────────────┘
              │
              ▼
     instantly revert to 100% on Revision N-1 — no redeploy needed,
     just repoint the traffic split
```

### Cold-Start Mitigation Beyond Image Size

- **`--min-instances 1`** (or higher) keeps at least one instance warm at all times — eliminates cold starts entirely for that baseline capacity, at the cost of paying for an always-on instance.
- **Startup CPU boost** (`--cpu-boost`) temporarily allocates extra CPU during container startup only, speeding up initialization-heavy services (e.g. those loading large in-memory caches) without paying for that CPU on every request.
- **Lazy-load non-critical dependencies**: initialize a database connection pool eagerly (needed for the first request), but defer anything not required to serve traffic (e.g. warming an analytics client) to a background goroutine after the server starts listening.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: Traffic splitting turns a deploy from a single all-or-nothing bet into a series of small, reversible bets — the same underlying idea as a canary deployment in Kubernetes (see the `kubernetes-zero-downtime-deployments` article), just expressed through `gcloud` tags and percentages instead of Service/Ingress objects.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.4: Knowledge Check — Cloud Run Production Readiness
lessons.body:
**Question 1:** Why does reducing container image size matter more on Cloud Run than on a long-running Kubernetes cluster?

A) Cloud Run doesn't support large images at all
B) Cloud Run must pull the image on every scale-from-zero cold start, while Kubernetes nodes typically already have images cached from prior pod scheduling
C) Image size affects billing but nothing else
D) It has no practical difference between the two platforms

**Correct answer: B.** Cold starts on Cloud Run include an image pull; a smaller image pulls faster, directly reducing the latency a user experiences when a new instance spins up from zero.

---

**Question 2:** What does `--vpc-egress private-ranges-only` actually route through the VPC connector?

A) All outbound traffic from the service, including calls to public APIs
B) Only traffic destined for RFC 1918 private IP ranges (like an internal Cloud SQL instance) — public API calls continue to egress normally
C) Only inbound traffic to the service
D) Nothing — it's a monitoring-only flag

**Correct answer: B.** `private-ranges-only` is the narrower of the two VPC egress settings — it's specifically for reaching private resources like Cloud SQL without paying the latency/cost of routing ALL traffic (including public API calls) through the connector.

---

**Question 3:** Why deploy a new revision with `--no-traffic --tag candidate` instead of letting `gcloud run deploy` route 100% of traffic immediately?

A) It's required by Cloud Run's API
B) It lets you gradually shift a small percentage of traffic to the new revision, observe its error rate, and instantly revert to the prior revision without a redeploy if something is wrong
C) It reduces the Docker image size
D) It's only useful for staging environments, never production

**Correct answer: B.** Deploying without traffic first, then using `update-traffic` to ramp a percentage up gradually, turns a risky all-at-once cutover into a small, reversible, observable rollout — the same principle behind canary deployments on any platform.
